title: The beaked plague doctor

traditional.note: A later account credits Charles de Lorme, physician to Louis XIII, with devising a full leather outfit during a Paris plague of 1619.

confidence.note: The attribution to Charles de Lorme rests on a later report, not a document from 1619. A 2020 museum study found no mention of the beak mask before the mid-17th century, then only in Italy and southern France, and doubts that the two surviving German masks were ever worn.

people: Charles de Lorme (1584–1678), physician to Louis XIII, credited with the idea
Thomas Bartholin (1616–1680), Danish physician who described the Roman costume
Paulus Fürst, publisher of the 1656 satirical print 'Der Doctor Schnabel von Rom'
summary: The beaked mask is a symbol of the Black Death, yet it first appears three centuries later, and there is little sign that many doctors ever wore one.
body: The beaked mask now stands for the Black Death, but no one wore it in the 1340s; medieval physicians held vinegar-soaked herbs to their noses. A beak holding perfumes before the nose is credited to Charles de Lorme, physician to Louis XIII, supposedly during a Paris plague of 1619. Firm evidence comes from Rome in 1656: the Danish physician Thomas Bartholin described Roman plague doctors in gowns of pressed linen with beaks stuffed with fragrant substances, and a German satirical print mocked 'Doctor Beaky of Rome'. The historian Marion Ruisinger found the mask recorded only in Italy and southern France, with no proof of its use in central Europe.

myth.tradition: Doctors in beaked masks tended victims of the Black Death in the 1340s.
myth.record: The beak mask is not mentioned before the mid-17th century, and even then only in Italy and southern France; the two masks in German museums show signs of never having been worn.

links.note: The pandemic the costume is wrongly linked with, three centuries earlier.

title: Harvey and the circulation of the blood

confidence.note: The printed book of 1628 survives and its arguments can be read today; the dates of publication and of Malpighi's capillaries are not in doubt. Credit for the pulmonary circuit belongs to earlier writers, but the full circulation is Harvey's.

people: William Harvey (1578–1657), physician and anatomist
Hieronymus Fabricius (1537–1619), Harvey's teacher at Padua, who described the valves in the veins
Marcello Malpighi, who saw the capillaries in 1661
summary: A London physician did the arithmetic: the heart pumps more blood in half an hour than the whole body holds. So the blood must go round.
body: In 1628 a slim Latin book of about 70 pages appeared in Frankfurt, written by William Harvey, physician to St Bartholomew's Hospital in London and to King James I. *Exercitatio anatomica de motu cordis et sanguinis in animalibus*, usually shortened to *De motu cordis*, argued that the heart is a pump and that the blood travels around the body in a circle, out through the arteries and back through the veins.

This overturned a system that had ruled European medicine for nearly 1,500 years. Galen taught that blood was made continually in the liver from digested food and was used up by the body's parts as nourishment, so it had to be replaced. It was a reasonable picture: food clearly becomes body. Harvey, who had studied at Padua under Fabricius, the anatomist who described the valves in the veins, attacked it with experiments on living animals and with a striking piece of arithmetic. Suppose, he wrote, the left ventricle throws out just half an ounce, or even one drachm, with each beat. In half an hour the heart beats more than a thousand times, so it moves more blood than the whole body contains. The liver could not make that much; the same blood must be going round.

Harvey could not see how blood crossed from the smallest arteries into the veins. That gap was closed in 1661, when Marcello Malpighi, using a microscope, saw the capillaries. Others had glimpsed part of the picture before him. In the 13th century the Arab physician Ibn al-Nafis described blood passing from the heart through the lungs and back, and in the 16th century Michael Servetus and Realdo Colombo argued for the same passage through the lungs.

Acceptance was slow but real. Conservative colleagues accused Harvey of quackery and his private practice suffered, yet by his death in 1657 circulation was widely accepted. Daily treatment barely changed. Purges and enemas built on Galen's physiology carried on, and Harvey himself still approved of bloodletting. Half a century after his death, Louis XIV of France had been bled 38 times. The discovery mattered first as a way of knowing: it showed that measurement and experiment could overturn the most revered authority in medicine. Its practical payoffs, such as blood transfusion, came later.

title: John Graunt counts the dead

confidence.note: The book and its tables survive and can be checked. Historians agree on its importance, but his famous survival table rests on many unstated assumptions and is not a life table in the modern actuarial sense.

people: John Graunt (1620–1674), London draper and author of the Observations
William Petty (1623–1687), physician and friend who coined 'political arithmetic' for such work
summary: A self-taught London draper turned the city's weekly death lists into the first serious numbers on who died, of what, and how young.
body: In 1662 John Graunt (1620–1674), a largely self-educated London draper, published *Natural and Political Observations ... upon the Bills of Mortality*. The Bills were weekly tallies of burials. Elderly women called searchers viewed each body and named a cause of death, and parish clerks printed the totals. Most readers scanned them only to see whether plague was rising, so they knew when to flee or how trade would suffer. Graunt saw that they could answer bigger questions.

Working mainly from the annual summaries of 1604–1660, and openly correcting for errors such as searchers bribed with ale to record syphilis as mere 'ulcers', he estimated London's population, showed that more boys are born than girls, measured migration from the countryside, and found that about a third of children died before age six. His table tracing the dying-out of a group of births is often called the first life table, but it rested on guesswork about ages; Edmond Halley later built one from real ages at death. The Royal Society elected Graunt a fellow, reportedly on the recommendation of Charles II.

myth.tradition: Graunt constructed the first life table.
myth.record: He was the first to describe, with many assumptions, the dying-out of a group of births, but without knowing ages at death; the first life table built on actual ages at death was Edmond Halley's.

links.note: A contemporary who also sorted diseases into kinds, and separated acute from chronic illness.
Counting deaths by cause became a tool of public health reform.
Plague years dominated the Bills that Graunt studied.

title: Thomas Willis maps the brain

confidence.note: *Cerebri Anatome* was printed in 1664 and its coinage of 'neurologia' can be read in it. Even his birthplace is reported differently by modern authors, but his book and its terms are not in doubt.

people: Thomas Willis (1621–1675), physician and anatomist

summary: An Oxford doctor dissected his own former patients, named the parts of the brain we still use, and coined the word 'neurology'.
body: In 1664 the Oxford physician Thomas Willis (1621–1675) published *Cerebri Anatome*, *The Anatomy of the Brain*, and in it coined 'neurologia', the doctrine of the nerves. Working largely from autopsies on his own former patients, he linked symptoms seen in life to structures found after death, and many of his names survive, among them the corpus striatum, the internal capsule and the vagus nerve. The ring of arteries at the base of the brain still bears his name. It was teamwork: Richard Lower and others prepared the brains, and Christopher Wren drew illustrations. A devout royalist, Willis hoped anatomy would reveal the workings of the soul.

links.note: Renaissance anatomy gave Willis his method of looking for himself.

title: Hooke, Leeuwenhoek and the invisible world

confidence.note: Hooke's book and Leeuwenhoek's letters to the Royal Society are dated and survive; 20th-century work confirmed that Leeuwenhoek really saw bacteria. What Kircher saw in plague blood is far less clear.

place: London, England, and Delft, Dutch Republic
people: Robert Hooke (1635–1703), curator of experiments at the Royal Society
Antoni van Leeuwenhoek (1632–1723), Delft draper and lens-maker
Henry Oldenburg, Royal Society secretary who translated and published Leeuwenhoek's letters
summary: A London experimenter drew a flea in its 'sable Armour'; a Delft cloth merchant found 'little animals' in rainwater. Medicine took two centuries to see why it mattered.
body: In 1665 Robert Hooke published *Micrographia*, a large illustrated book of what his compound microscope revealed: a flea in its polished 'suite of sable Armour', and in thin slices of cork, rows of tiny boxes he called 'cells'. It became a bestseller. Samuel Pepys stayed up until two in the morning reading it and called it the most ingenious book he had ever read, while a satirist mocked Hooke for spending a fortune to study mites in cheese.

Across the North Sea, the Delft cloth merchant Antoni van Leeuwenhoek, who had probably seen *Micrographia*, was grinding his own tiny single lenses. He made more than 500 instruments, simple but powerful magnifiers that enlarged over 200 times, far beyond the 20 or 30 times of early compound microscopes. In a letter of October 1676 to the Royal Society, published in 1677, he reported 'living creatures in Rain water', the first detailed description of what we now call protists and bacteria. In 1683 he described similar creatures in the white matter scraped from between his teeth.

London was skeptical. Christiaan Huygens suspected illusions of sight. The Royal Society asked the botanist Nehemiah Grew to repeat the work, and he failed; Hooke succeeded only at his third attempt, in 1677. Leeuwenhoek, an unschooled tradesman who kept his methods secret, gathered signed statements from eight respectable witnesses to vouch for what he had seen.

Medicine took little notice. The idea of invisible disease-causing seeds was ancient, and the Jesuit scholar Athanasius Kircher (1602–1680) thought he saw 'worms' in the blood of plague victims and blamed them for the disease. But such claims could not be fitted into the reigning theories of bad air and imbalanced humors, which held until the 19th century. Because no one could match the clarity of Leeuwenhoek's lenses, his discoveries were doubted for generations. It was Louis Pasteur and Robert Koch, nearly two centuries later, who tied microbes to disease.

myth.tradition: No one imagined that tiny living things caused disease before Pasteur.
myth.record: The idea is ancient, and Kircher blamed microscopic 'worms' for plague in the 17th century; what was missing was proof, and a theory of disease that could make use of it.

links.note: Fracastoro's 'seeds' of contagion were an earlier guess at invisible causes.

title: The first blood transfusions

confidence.note: The London experiments are recorded in the Royal Society's minutes and in Pepys's diary. Whether the human recipients were helped or simply survived is another matter.

people: Richard Lower, Oxford and London physician
Edmund King, physician who performed the London human transfusion with Lower
Jean-Baptiste Denis, Paris physician
summary: Within 40 years of Harvey, doctors were piping blood from dog to dog, then sheep to man. One volunteer was paid 20 shillings and said he felt 'a new man'.
body: Harvey's circulation invited a bold next step. In 1665 Richard Lower kept a dog alive with blood from other dogs, and on 14 November 1666 the Royal Society watched one dog bled to death into another, which survived. In 1667 Jean-Baptiste Denis in Paris, and Lower and Edmund King in London, put sheep's blood into people. The London volunteer, a poor and 'a little frantic' former minister, was paid 20 shillings; afterwards he said he felt 'much better', though Pepys thought him 'cracked a little in his head'. Transfusion between humans came only in 1818, when James Blundell tried it for bleeding after childbirth.

links.note: Circulation made transfusion thinkable.

title: Sydenham at the bedside

confidence.note: His books and their dates are not in doubt. His stature as the 'English Hippocrates' was largely a later verdict; in his lifetime he was at odds with the medical establishment.

people: Thomas Sydenham (1624–1689), London physician
summary: A Puritan ex-soldier told doctors to stop theorizing and watch their patients. He became the 'English Hippocrates', but only after he died.
body: Thomas Sydenham (1624–1689) came from a Puritan family, fought for Parliament in the Civil War and practised in London outside the universities. Influenced by Francis Bacon, he argued that diseases should be understood from close observation of their signs and course, not from theories about hidden mechanisms. His *Observationes Medicae* of 1676 expanded a 1666 book on fevers into a system of 'epidemic constitutions' shaped by season and environment, and his sorting of diseases into distinct kinds helped found nosology. His accounts of gout, which he suffered for 30 years, and of the childhood chorea that bears his name became classics. He preferred diet to aggressive bloodletting.

title: The royal touch

confidence.note: Eyewitnesses such as Pepys describe the ceremony, and court registers recorded the numbers. The totals come from later compilers and differ slightly: 92,107 between 1660 and 1682 in one count, 'near a hundred thousand' over the reign in another.

people: Charles II (reigned 1660–1685), who touched more sufferers than any other English monarch on record
Samuel Pepys (1633–1703), diarist and eyewitness
Samuel Johnson, touched as a small child by Queen Anne
summary: Charles II laid hands on some 90,000 sick subjects to cure the 'king's evil'. In 1684 the crowd was so thick that several were trampled to death.
body: On 23 June 1660, weeks after his restoration, Charles II was due to touch the sick at Whitehall. It rained, and the poor stood all morning in the garden before he touched them in the Banqueting House. English and French monarchs claimed a God-given power to cure scrofula, the 'king's evil', by laying on hands and hanging a gold coin round the sufferer's neck. Demand was immense: one count gives 92,107 people touched between 1660 and 1682, and in 1684 several were trampled to death in the crush. William III called it 'a silly superstition', but Queen Anne still touched, among others the infant Samuel Johnson, without effect.

myth.tradition: The English royal touch goes back to Edward the Confessor.
myth.record: The ceremony was traditionally traced to Edward the Confessor, but there is no direct evidence that the early Norman kings touched for the evil.

title: Ramazzini and the diseases of workers

confidence.note: The 1700 and 1713 editions survive. His medicine drew on ancient authorities rather than new anatomy, but his systematic survey of trades is not in doubt.

people: Bernardino Ramazzini (1633–1714), professor of medicine at Modena and Padua
summary: An Italian professor went into the workshops and found millers half-deaf and midwives worn out. His 1700 survey of 40 trades founded occupational medicine.
body: In 1700 Bernardino Ramazzini (1633–1714), professor of medicine at Modena, published *De Morbis Artificum Diatriba*, a treatise on the diseases of workers covering some 40 occupations. Each chapter described a trade and its workplace, the questions to put to its workers, their diseases and the remedies. Corn millers, he wrote, were nearly all 'half-deaf' from the noise of wheels and millstones; midwives spent hours on their knees and risked infection from their patients. He suggested crude earplugs and thorough washing, and argued that rulers should protect workers' health. An enlarged edition appeared in 1713, the year before his death in Padua.

links.note: Ramazzini followed the revived Hippocratic approach of Sydenham.
Work and living conditions became a target of public health.
